abbreviate

/uh-BREE-vee-ayt/ - the stress falls on BREE · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Abbreviate means to shorten a word or phrase.

Knitting patterns abbreviate every instruction, so 'k2tog' saves the line that 'knit two together' would fill.

Example

The scoreboard operator had four letter spaces per team, so she learned to abbreviate even the proudest school names: Sacred Heart Academy of the Valley lit up simply as SHAV.

Abbreviate is the precise choice because it works on words, phrases and names — usually crushing them to initials or a clipped form — while abridge or condense describe shrinking a whole text, not a label.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

clip: To clip is to chop a piece off a word's end — 'gymnasium' keeps its head and loses its tail to become 'gym.' Abbreviate covers far more ground: initials, symbols, and clipped forms alike, shrinking whole phrases and names, not just one word's tail.

contract: To contract is to squeeze a word by dropping middle letters, usually marking the gap with an apostrophe — 'do not' becomes 'don't.' Abbreviate is broader and needs no apostrophe: it shortens any word, phrase, or name into initials or a clipped written form.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lengthen: to make longer rather than shorter

elongate: to stretch something out, usually a physical thing

Where it sits · how drastically the wording is compressed — trim → shorten → abbreviate

trim vs. abbreviate: To trim is the gentlest cut of all — a little off the edges — and it stops far short of abbreviate, which can flatten a whole title into letters.

shorten vs. abbreviate: Shorten goes further than trim, dropping real chunks, but abbreviate is this ladder's extreme: it can crush a three-word company name down to three letters.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ab-

Prefix — ab-: to, toward (Latin ad-, reshaped before b)

Root — brevi

Root — brevi: short (Latin brevis)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make

Put it together

Put it together: Ab- here is Latin ad- ('to') in disguise: before a b, ad- shifted its spelling, so abbreviare meant 'to bring to shortness' — brevi- ('short') plus the verb-making -ate. When you abbreviate a phrase, you are literally making it short.

Use the root in a new word: brevity

Use the root in a new word: brevity: The editor praised the report's brevity: every fact was there, and not one extra sentence.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / technical

Reach for abbreviate when a word, phrase or name gets a shorter written form — initials, a clipped word, a symbol. If a whole book or report is being shrunk while keeping its content, that is abridge, this unit's other shortening word; and condense is the everyday word for squeezing anything denser.
